args.body:
PRIVILEGED AND CONFIDENTIAL — ATTORNEY WORK PRODUCT
PREPARED IN ANTICIPATION OF LITIGATION

MEMORANDUM

TO:      Engagement Team — White Collar Defense Investigations
FROM:    [Firm Counsel]
DATE:    [Current Date]
RE:      Negotiation Analysis — Government Counter-Markup of Deferred Prosecution Agreement
         (Financial Services Company) — Matter File 26

--------------------------------------------------------------------------
I. EXECUTIVE SUMMARY
--------------------------------------------------------------------------

We have reviewed the government's counter-markup of the Deferred Prosecution Agreement
("DPA") for our financial services client against the original DPA and our initial markup
(the "base materials"). The government's counter-markup accepts most of the firm-standard
provisions reflected in our initial markup, but it introduces three material deviations that
must be reconciled against the base materials, the qualifying disclosure schedules, and the
controlling instructions of the deal team:

  1. A reduction of the indemnification cap combined with the conversion of the deductible
     (basket) into a tipping basket;
  2. New Material Adverse Effect ("MAE") carve-outs for regulatory action of exactly the kind
     at issue in this matter; and
  3. A new limitation period that shortens the survival of the core representations.

Our analysis of the government's counter-markup is governed by the client's controlling
negotiation priorities, as confirmed by the most recent (controlling) partner instruction on
this engagement:

  • The client will CONCEDE the basket conversion (converting the deductible into a tipping
    basket); and
  • The client treats ANY reduction in the survival period of the core representations as a
    WALK-AWAY item.

This memo analyzes each deviation against the original DPA and our initial markup, cross-
references the qualifying disclosure schedules, identifies the risk each change presents, and
recommends a negotiation posture (accept / reject / counter) consistent with the client's
controlling priorities.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------
II. BACKGROUND AND DEAL OVERVIEW
--------------------------------------------------------------------------

The engagement concerns the negotiation of a DPA between our client, a financial services
company, and the government. The operative agreement, as contemplated by the base materials,
contains the following core categories of provisions: representations and warranties;
affirmative and negative covenants; conditions to closing/effective date; indemnification and
claims process; and termination and survival provisions. The parties have negotiated these
provisions through successive markups.

The transaction history relevant to this analysis is as follows:

  • Original DPA. The government's baseline form of DPA, which served as the starting point
    for our initial markup.
  • Our Initial Markup. Our response to the original DPA incorporating firm-standard
    provisions and client-favorable formulations, many of which the government has now
    accepted in the counter-markup.
  • Government Counter-Markup. The government's latest response, which accepts most
    firm-standard provisions but introduces the three material deviations identified above.

Because the government's counter-markup was prepared on the assumption that our client would
carry forward certain exposures, counsel must ensure that the scheduled exceptions — which by
their terms control over general statements in the base materials — are fully reconciled before
the DPA is executed.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------
III. CONTROLLING NEGOTIATION INSTRUCTIONS AND PRIORITIES
--------------------------------------------------------------------------

The deal team correspondence on this engagement sets the analytical framework for the memo.
The most recent message in the thread REVISES the analysis priorities and is the controlling
instruction; it supersedes all earlier messages in the thread that stated the opposite priority
ordering.

Controlling priorities:

  • Basket Conversion — CONCEDE. The client will concede the government's conversion of the
    indemnification deductible (basket) from a deductible into a tipping basket. We should not
    spend negotiation capital resisting this point.

  • Survival-Period Reduction — WALK-AWAY. The client treats any reduction in the survival
    period of the core representations as a walk-away issue. This is the client's
    non-negotiable line; a shortening of survival for the core representations is
    unacceptable.

These two priorities materially drive our recommended positions below and should be treated as
binding on the negotiating team.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------
IV. DEVIATION-BY-DEVIATION ANALYSIS
--------------------------------------------------------------------------

DEVIATION 1 — INDEMNIFICATION CAP AND BASKET (DEDUCTIBLE → TIPPING BASKET)
--------------------------------------------------------------------------

What the government proposes. The government's counter-markup (i) silently reduces the
indemnification cap and (ii) converts the indemnification basket from a deductible into a
tipping basket.

Comparison with the base materials. Under the original DPA and our initial markup, the parties
operated on a higher indemnification cap together with a deductible structure: the client bore
losses up to the deductible threshold before any indemnity obligation attached (a true
deductible). The government's counter-markup reduces the cap and converts the structure to a
tipping basket, under which once losses cross the (lowered or unchanged) threshold the client
is responsible for the entire amount from the first dollar.

Analysis and risk. The conversion to a tipping basket is more onerous than a deductible because
it obligates the client to absorb the full amount of covered losses from the first dollar once
the threshold is exceeded, rather than only the excess over the threshold. The simultaneous
reduction of the cap further increases the client's net exposure. In a DPA context, however,
"indemnification" commonly refers to the client's agreement to pay penalties, restitution, and
disgorgement, and the basket/cap mechanics govern the trigger and ceiling for those payments.

Reconciling the disclosure schedules. Schedule 5.2 lists retained liabilities that the
government's indemnification changes would silently shift onto the client. Because scheduled
exceptions control over general statements in the base materials, we must confirm that the
identified retained liabilities remain excluded from (or are priced into) any shifted
obligation. If the indemnification changes are applied without reconciling Schedule 5.2, the
client could unknowingly assume additional liability for the retained items.

Recommended posture — ACCEPT the basket conversion (concede), CONDITIONAL on the cap
adjustment. Consistent with the client's controlling instruction to concede the basket
conversion, we should not oppose the deductible-to-tipping-basket change. However, we should
resist the silent reduction of the indemnification cap unless it is acceptable to the client,
and we must ensure that Schedule 5.2 retained liabilities are expressly carved out of any
shifted obligation. Our counter should: (a) accept the tipping basket; (b) return the cap to
the level reflected in our initial markup unless a concession is planned; and (c) add a
carve-out confirming that Schedule 5.2 retained liabilities are not covered by the
indemnification.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------

DEVIATION 2 — MATERIAL ADVERSE EFFECT ("MAE") CARVE-OUTS FOR REGULATORY ACTION
--------------------------------------------------------------------------

What the government proposes. The government's counter-markup adds carve-outs to the
definition of Material Adverse Effect for regulatory action of exactly the kind at issue in
this matter.

Comparison with the base materials. The original DPA and our initial markup defined MAE without
the broad regulatory-action carve-outs the government now seeks. The carve-outs would treat as
outside the definition of MAE (and therefore outside any protection based on an MAE) adverse
consequences arising from regulatory action of the type that is central to this matter.

Analysis and risk. The carve-outs are designed to neutralize the MAE protection precisely where
our client is most exposed. This is the most analytically significant deviation, because it is
not merely a monetary adjustment but a substantive redefinition of a core protective concept
that intersects directly with the pending regulatory inquiries our client faces.

Reconciling the disclosure schedules. Schedule 3.7 discloses two pending regulatory inquiries
that intersect the government's proposed MAE carve-outs. The scheduled exceptions control over
general statements in the base materials. Because the pending inquiries are the exact "kind" of
regulatory action the government seeks to carve out, the government's proposed carve-outs would
strip protection for the very risk that the schedules identify. This is unacceptable unless the
carve-outs are drafted narrowly so that they do not capture the specific inquiries disclosed in
Schedule 3.7 or otherwise alter the intended risk allocation.

Recommended posture — REJECT / HEAVILY COUNTER. The MAE carve-outs should be rejected as
drafted. At minimum, we should counter with carve-out language that expressly excludes the two
pending regulatory inquiries disclosed in Schedule 3.7, and that limits the carve-outs to
regulatory action outside the ordinary course or not specifically disclosed. We should insist
that the scheduled exceptions control and that the carve-outs cannot be applied to the pending
inquiries. This item is a priority negotiation point and may be used as a trading chip only if
necessary, but should not be conceded without a corresponding value exchange.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------

DEVIATION 3 — LIMITATION PERIOD / SURVIVAL OF CORE REPRESENTATIONS
--------------------------------------------------------------------------

What the government proposes. The government's counter-markup introduces a new limitation
period that shortens the survival of the core representations.

Comparison with the base materials. Exhibit B to the base materials sets the survival matrix
for the representations and warranties. The government's limitation-period change directly
contradicts the survival matrix in Exhibit B. Under the original DPA and our initial markup, the
core representations carried the survival periods prescribed by Exhibit B; the government's
change would shorten those periods for the core representations.

Analysis and risk. A shortened survival period materially reduces the client's protection under
the DPA by limiting the window during which claims, adjustments, or clawbacks can be raised
based on the core representations. Shorter survival also undermines the predictability of the
risk allocation that the parties had already negotiated.

Reconciling the disclosure schedules. Exhibit B controls the survival matrix, and scheduled
exceptions control over general statements in the base materials. The government's limitation-
period change contradicts Exhibit B and therefore should not be accepted unless the survival
matrix is amended in conjunction.

Recommended posture — REJECT / WALK-AWAY. Per the client's controlling instruction, any
reduction in the survival period of the core representations is a walk-away item. We should
therefore reject the government's limitation-period change in full and hold firm to the
survival matrix in Exhibit B. This is the client's stated deal-breaker; we should communicate
clearly to the government that accepting the shortened survival period is a precondition to
our continued willingness to negotiate. There is no counter that cures a walk-away item — we
recommend holding the line.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------
V. CUMULATIVE RISK ASSESSMENT
--------------------------------------------------------------------------

Taken together, the government's counter-markup would:
  • Increase the client's net financial exposure through the cap reduction and the
    deductible-to-tipping-basket conversion (mitigated by our conceded basket);
  • Strip MAE protection in precisely the area of the client's disclosed regulatory exposure
    (Schedule 3.7), unless the carve-outs are narrowed; and
  • Shorten the survival of the core representations in contravention of the agreed survival
    matrix (Exhibit B), which the client has identified as a walk-away item.

The combination of the cap reduction and the MAE carve-outs is of particular concern because
both operate silently and would, without scheduled reconciliation, expand the client's
exposure on the matters already disclosed in Schedule 5.2 (retained liabilities) and Schedule
3.7 (pending regulatory inquiries).

--------------------------------------------------------------------------
VI. COMPARATIVE SUMMARY (ORIGINAL DPA vs. OUR INITIAL MARKUP vs. GOVT COUNTER-MARKUP)
--------------------------------------------------------------------------

Provision                       | Original DPA      | Our Initial Markup      | Gov't Counter-Markup         | Recommended Posture
--------------------------------|-------------------|-------------------------|------------------------------|----------------------------
Indemnification cap             | Baseline cap      | Higher/firm-standard cap | Silently reduced             | Counter — hold cap level
Basket structure                | Deductible        | Deductible              | Tipping basket              | ACCEPT (concede)
MAE definition                  | No regulatory carve-out(s) | No broad carve-outs | Adds regulatory-action carve-outs | REJECT/counter (narrow to exclude Sched. 3.7)
Survival / limitation period    | Exhibit B matrix  | Exhibit B matrix        | Shortened (contradicts Ex. B) | REJECT — walk-away item
Retained liabilities (Sched. 5.2) | Retained        | Carved out             | Silently shifted by indemn. changes | Ensure carve-out retained

--------------------------------------------------------------------------
VII. RECOMMENDED NEGOTIATION PLAN AND NEXT STEPS
--------------------------------------------------------------------------

1. Concede the basket conversion (tipping basket) as instructed. Reflect this concession
   expressly in the next markup.

2. Hold the indemnification cap at the level in our initial markup and, in parallel, confirm
   that Schedule 5.2 retained liabilities remain expressly carved out of any shifted
   indemnification obligation.

3. Reject the MAE carve-outs as drafted and counter with narrow carve-out language that
   expressly excludes the two pending regulatory inquiries disclosed in Schedule 3.7. Confirm
   that the scheduled exceptions control.

4. Reject the survival-period reduction in full. Treat any shortening of the survival period
   of the core representations (contradicting Exhibit B) as a walk-away item, consistent with
   the controlling partner instruction. Do not counter this item; instead communicate the
   client's position as a precondition to further negotiation.

5. Before execution, reconcile BOTH the disclosure schedules (Schedules 3.7 and 5.2) and
   Exhibit B against the final conformed DPA to ensure the scheduled exceptions control and no
   silent shift of liability occurs.

We recommend advancing the above positions in the next markup and resisting any packaging that
ties the conceded basket to the walk-away survival item. Should the government make the survival
reduction a condition of further negotiation, we are instructed to treat that as a walk-away.

Please let us know if you would like us to prepare a conformed redline implementing these
positions.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------
[Privileged & Confidential — Prepared in Anticipation of Negotiation/Litigation]
